newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis, Palestinians clash over tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Israelis, Palestinians clash over tunnel.

text.p: Palestinians clashed with police on Tuesday after Israeli workmen under cover of night and heavy police guard opened a tunnel beside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, site of Islam's third holiest shrine.

Police said they fired rubber bullets to disperse youths throwing stones and bottles and briefly evacuated Jewish worshippers from the Wailing Wall after stones were hurled from the Temple Mount above.
The clashes were reminiscent of the Palestinian uprising or intifada and highlighted the deteriorating relations between Arabs and the new right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In the West Bank city of Hebron Israeli soliders broke up a separate demonstration by 500 Palestinians, beating several and arresting four, witnesses said. Prominent Palestinian Hanan Ashrawi was pushed to the ground in a scuffle with soldiers who were prevented from arresting her by demonstrators, they said.

The protests in Jerusalem started after labourers opened an entrance on the Via Dolorosa to a narrow tourist tunnel running 488 metres (500 yards) along the Wailing Wall, a retaining wall of the ruined Second Jewish Temple, now a Moslem site.
"This is a crime, a big crime against our religious and holy places," Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in Palestinian-ruled Gaza.
"This (is) Israeli madness to change the features of Jerusalem," Arafat told reporters.

Israel said the opening to the existing tunnel would allow tourists easier access to archaeological sites beneath the Wailing Wall, Judaism's holiest site. The Israeli government said the second entrance would allow 400,000 tourists a year to use the tunnel whereas now only 70,000 a year have been able to squeeze through the metre-wide opening which serves as both entrance and exit.
Several hundred Palestinians surged along the Via Dolorosa to the tunnel entrance but were held back by police. Arab merchants shuttered their stores in a protest strike.

Police said several Arabs threw stones at officers on the Temple Mount and at Jews at the Wailing Wall below. Similar stone-throwing six years ago led to police storming the Temple Mount complex and shooting dead 17 Palestinians.

On Tuesday, clashes spilled out of the walled Old City to other parts of Arab East Jerusalem. Youths threw stones and set fire to a truck off Salah-a-Din Street, the main commercial thoroughfare. Police responded with rubber bullets and arrested more than a dozen protesters.
Clashes also erupted in the village of Silwan, below the city walls, after Jewish settlers moved into a house, residents said.
The Temple Mount, known to Moslems as Haram al-Sharif, houses the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa mosques. It is a flashpoint in the Israeli-Palestinian struggle.

Jerusalem is one of the most explosive issues still to be tackled in Israeli-Palestinian peace talks which have already snagged on supposedly easier issues such as Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron.
Netanyahu's handling of the peace talks have led to plummeting relations with the Palestinians and tensions with Egypt, Syria and Lebanon.

The future of East Jerusalem, which Palestinians want as the capital of an independent Palestine, was to be negotiated under an Israeli-Palestinian accord signed in 1993. However, Netanyahu, who took office in June, has refused to discuss relinquishing control of East Jerusalem which Israel captured in 1967.
Senior Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters that policies like the opening of the controversial tunnel "push the Palestinians and Israelis towards...confrontation and catastrophe."

Israeli archaeological digging on the edges of the Temple Mount, including the tunnel, have long aroused charges in the Arab world that they are part of a campaign to strengthen Israeli control and undermine Moslem sacred sites.
